read.passage: Few crafts are as closely woven into the fabric of Arabian life as Al-Sadu, the Bedouin art of weaving wool from sheep, camels and goats. For generations, the skill was handed down from grandmother to granddaughter, and its bold geometric patterns decorated tents, cushions and camel saddles. As families settled in cities, however, Sadu came close to becoming a dying art. Critics of recent revivals contend that printing Sadu patterns on phone cases and notebooks reduces a living tradition to a decorative trend. Supporters concede that some products are superficial, but maintain that a tradition frozen in time is more likely to disappear than one that adapts. Were young designers to stop experimenting, they argue, Sadu would survive only in museums.

qs.q: Why did Sadu come close to disappearing?
options: Families moved to cities and the skill was passed on less.
UNESCO banned its use on tents.

qs.q: What do critics of the revival argue?
options: Sadu should be taught in every school.
That museums are the best place for Sadu
That adapting a tradition always destroys it
That some modern products are superficial

qs.q: According to supporters, what would happen if designers stopped experimenting?
options: Sadu would survive only in museums.
